scenario_provenance.archetype_label: Multi-focus on Practices 3 & 4 (analyze data; interpret results)
validity_rules: OBSERVATIONAL comparison only (no random assignment -> no causal claim)
means differ but spreads overlap so an over-strong claim is refutable

sources.note: the item stem's verb must match the scored demand

prompt: In an observational garden study, plants in sunny spots had a mean recorded height of 60 cm (SD about 10) and plants in shaded spots had a mean of 55 cm (SD about 10). A student claims: "plants in sunny spots always have a higher recorded height than plants in shaded spots." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

options.text: On average plants in sunny spots had a higher recorded height (mean 60 vs 55), so the data support a typical difference; but because both SDs are about 10, the distributions overlap substantially, so the data do not support a claim that plants in sunny spots are always higher.
These results prove that plants in sunny spots will always outperform plants in shaded spots on recorded height in any future study or population.

misconception_source.label: Over-generalized beyond the data using definitive language

sources.note: 2025 CR Report: conclusions must use non-definitive language ('convincing evidence'), never 'proves'/'always'; and must not generalize beyond the studied population

options.text: The claim is correct because plants in sunny spots clearly did better on recorded height.

misconception_source.label: Restated the claim without citing statistical evidence

sources.ref: AP_STATISTICS_2027_CED_FACT_PACK.md S4/S6 (skill 4.B; task verbs) + S10 'General exam-wide conventions'
sources.note: a justification must reference the statistical evidence, not merely restate the claim

options.text: Because plants in sunny spots had a higher mean recorded height, being in plants in sunny spots causes a higher recorded height.

misconception_source.label: Interpreted an observational association as causation

sources.note: EK 5.2.A.4: correlation does not imply causation (stated explicitly)
observational studies (no random assignment) do not support causal claims

parts.prompt: In an observational garden study, plants in sunny spots had a mean recorded height of 60 cm (SD about 10) and plants in shaded spots had a mean of 55 cm (SD about 10). A student claims: "plants in sunny spots always have a higher recorded height than plants in shaded spots." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

criteria.description: Selects the justification that affirms the on-average difference while rejecting the over-strong 'always' claim due to overlap.
